CHAPTER TWENTY-FOUR.

3222. Moreover, loves and their affections are represented by flames, and this with inexpressible variation; but truths are represented by lights, and by innumerable modifications of light. From this it can be evident why, in the Word, flames signify the goods of love, and lights signify the truths of faith.

3223. There are two lights by which man is illuminated: the light of the world and the light of heaven. The light of the world is from the sun; the light of heaven is from the Lord. The light of the world is for the natural or external man, and thus for those things that are within him. The things that are there, even though they do not appear to belong to that light, still exist, for nothing can be grasped by the natural man except through such things as exist and appear in the solar world, and thus unless they have some form through light and shadow there. All ideas of time and ideas of space, which make up so much of the natural man that he cannot think without them, also belong to the light of the world. However, the light of heaven is for the spiritual or internal man. The interior mind of man, where his intellectual ideas—which are called immaterial—reside, is in that light. Man does not know this, even though he calls his intellect "sight" and ascribes light to it. The reason is that, as long as he is in worldly and bodily things, he has perception only of such things as are of the light of the world, and not of such as are of the light of heaven. The light of heaven is from the Lord alone; the universal heaven is in that light. This light, namely the light of heaven, is immensely more perfect than the light of the world. The things that form one ray in the light of the world form myriads in the light of heaven. In the light of heaven is intelligence and wisdom. That light is what flows into the light of the world, which is in the external or natural man, and causes him to perceive the objects of things sensually. Unless that light flowed in, man would have no perception at all, for life from that source is within the things that are of the light of the world. Between these lights, or between those things that are in the light of heaven and in the light of the world, there is a correspondence when the external or natural man makes one with the internal or spiritual, that is, when the former serves the latter; and the things that then exist in the light of the world are representative of such things as are in the light of heaven.

3224. It is remarkable that man does not yet know that his intellectual mind is in a certain light which is entirely different from the light of the world. But such is the condition that, to those who are in the light of the world, the light of heaven is as it were darkness, and to those who are in the light of heaven, the light of the world is as it were darkness. This comes principally from loves, which are the heats of light. Those who are in the loves of self and of the world, and thus in the heat of the light of the world alone, are affected only by evils and falsities, and these are what extinguish the truths that are of the light of heaven. <summary>This passage defines the distinction between the light of the world and the light of heaven, explaining that the latter is the source of all intellectual perception and wisdom, while the former serves as the natural vessel for these spiritual influxes.</summary>
